Prologue.

How, with the appetite for more knowledge, our first parents deserved to be deprived of the original knowledge that had been given to them, and to fall into the very dark night of ignorance in which they left all of us. Not having yet lost that cursed appetite, we do not cease to persist in wanting to investigate, by fair means or foul, what we do not know, both concerning natural things and concerning supernatural things. And although to learn many of these things we have many and very reliable paths, we are not content with this; instead, through unlawful and forbidden paths, we seek to know things that our Lord God is not pleased for us to know: such as future things and secret things. And this is done sometimes through the way of the demon, at other times by conjecturing from the roars of animals, or the cries of birds, or the appearance of certain creeping things. This is an evil that has spread throughout the whole human race, and since these natives have a good share of it, we may say they are quite afflicted by this sickness. And so that, when those who are wounded by this affliction come seeking a cure, the physician may easily understand them, the present book sets forth many of the omens that these natives used to observe; and at the end it deals with various kinds of ancient apparitions that used to appear to them at night.

Book Five, which speaks of
the omens: that these Mexican
people used.

Chapter One: concerning the omen
they took: when someone heard at night
some fierce beast howling,
or crying like an old woman: and about
what the omen-readers said in this
case.

In times past,
before the Spaniards came
to this land: the natives of it
had many omens: by which
they divined future things.

The first of these omens is:
that when someone heard in the
mountains some fierce beast roar,
or some sound making a buzzing
in the mountains or in the valleys:
they would then take it as a bad omen,
saying that it meant some
misfortune or disaster that was going
to befall them.

This is the fifth book, in which is told
the omens that the Mexica held
to be fearful and that frightened them.

This is the first chapter, in which is told
the omen that frightened them: when
at night someone heard
some wild beast crying out, or likewise
an old woman crying: and then
whatever the soothsayers said about it
is here related, as the wise men
held it to be.

Long ago, in the time when the fire still smoldered,
thus it is said, certain
old men, aged people,
said: when we were still blind,
when we were still foolish, when we
dwelt upon the earth, we used to say
that there were things which befell us,
things which came upon us. All these
things they held to be omens, they regarded
them with fear; they knew the omen as
something to be feared, as something
portending misfortune.

As for the first thing, it was this: when
someone heard a wild beast cry out, a wild
beast crying over something; or likewise
when a conch shell was blown; when a mountain
responded with an echo; when something
howled or screeched; or when an old woman
cried out like that. This, they said, meant
that war would come, or that someone would die,
would perish in war; or that something would
befall one; so [it was believed].

Book Five

...of coming soon, or that he was to
die in war, or of sickness,
or that some disaster or misfortune
was to come to him: or that he
was to be made a slave, either he himself or
one of his children, or that some mis-
fortune was to befall him, or his
household. Having heard this evil
omen, he would go at once to seek out
those who knew how to interpret these
omens, whom they called tonalpouhque
(day-readers). And this omen-reader, or diviner,
would console and encourage such a person,
speaking to him in this manner: "My poor
little son: since you have come to seek
the interpretation of the omen that you saw,
and you came to look into the mirror where
the interpretation of what you saw is found,
know that what this omen of yours signifies
is an adverse and troublesome thing. And this
is not because I say so, but because thus it was
left said and written by our elders and
ancestors regarding the meaning of this omen
of yours: that you are to find yourself in
poverty and hardship, or you will die. Perhaps
it has already been decreed against you by him
through whom we live, and he no longer wishes
you to live; and it is already determined in his
mind what is to befall you, because thus it is
written in our books which we use to
interpret these things, to which it
happens. And this — it is not I who instill
fear or dread in you — for it was the Lord
God Himself who willed that this should befall
you and come upon you; and there is no one
to blame for it, because he [the omen] does not
know what he does, for he lacks understanding
and reason; and you, poor little one, must not
blame anyone, because..."

[The Nahuatl text continues, paralleling and elaborating upon the same theme in the original language — the diviner's words of consolation to the poor man who has received a bad omen, speaking of poverty, servitude, affliction, weariness, and resignation to the will of the Lord by whom all live, urging the person to take heart, endure what has been foretold by the sign of his birth-day (tonalli), and accept with patience and courage the hardships, grief, and misfortune that are to come, for such is the decree of the Lord our God, and he must bear it bravely, strengthen his heart, and not fail under the weight of his sorrow.]

Of the Omens fo. 2.

The sign under which you were born carries with it these misfortunes, which have now come. Now you must verify for yourself the evil of the sign under which you were born. Take heart, because through experience you will feel it; see that you have good courage to endure it, and meanwhile weep and do penance. Note what I will now tell you to do to remedy your trouble or your misfortune: do penance; seek paper so that your offering, which you must make, may be prepared; buy paper, and burn it black and with rubber, and the other things you know are necessary for this offering. After you have prepared what is needed, you will see which day is suitable for making the offering, which is required for the lord, the fire god; then you shall come to me, because I myself will lay out and arrange the papers and everything else, in the places and manner in which they must be for making the offering. I myself must go to light and burn it in your house. In this way did those who heard the aforementioned omen act.

Second Chapter, on the indifferent omen that was taken from hearing a bird sing, called oacton, and about what the merchants who traveled on the road did in this case.

The second omen they had was when they heard a bird sing or chatter, which they called oactli, or oacton. This omen was indifferent, for sometimes it foretold well and sometimes badly. They considered it good when it sang as if laughing, because then it seemed to say "ieccan, ieccan," which means "good time, good time." When in this manner...

[Nahuatl text, parallel in content to the Spanish, describing the rites of offering incense, paper, and rubber to the fire god to remedy the ill omen of one's birth sign, the proper timing and manner of making offerings in the house, and the account of the omen-bearing bird oactli — how its cry, laughter-like or otherwise, was interpreted by merchants traveling the road as a sign of good or bad fortune, with certain calls taken as auspicious ("ieccan, ieccan") bringing joy and causing travelers to proceed without fear.]

Book Five

...continually they had no suspicion that any harm would come, rather they rejoiced to hear it, because they believed that some good fortune was about to befall them. But when they heard this bird that sang or chattered — like someone laughing with great laughter and a loud voice, and whose laughter seemed to come from deep within the chest, like someone who feels great joy and happiness — then they would fall silent and grow faint. No one spoke to another; all walked along silently and with heads bowed, because they understood that some evil was about to come upon them, or that one of them was going to die soon, or that one of them was going to fall ill, or that they were going to be captured by those into whose lands they were traveling.

This happened for the most part in certain deep valleys, or at certain great streams, or in certain great mountains, or in certain great wastelands. If the travelers who heard this were merchants or traders, they would say among themselves: "Some evil is about to befall us — some flood of a river, or flash flood, is going to sweep us away, or our cargo; or we are going to fall into the hands of thieves who will rob or assault us; or perhaps one of us will fall ill and we will have to leave him abandoned; or perhaps wild beasts will devour us, or..."

[Nahuatl column, parallel text, describing the same omen of the bird whose call presages misfortune — whether sickness, death, captivity, or other evil was about to happen to them, whether in the mountains, ravines, plains, forests, or dark woods; and that this happened to merchants and travelers when they heard the owl laughing, which they took to mean that calamity, drowning, enslavement, robbery, or similar misfortunes were about to come upon them.]

Of the omens.

...fortune may lead us to cut short some
war, so that we cannot
pass through. When they discussed these
matters among themselves, the one who was the
leader among them would begin to
encourage and console the others,
the lesser ones, and he would speak to them in this
manner as they went along walking: "My sons,
and my brothers, none of you
should be saddened, nor lose heart,
because of the omen you have heard; for
we already understood this when
we left our houses
and our kinfolk, that we
came to offer ourselves to death.
And their tears and their weeping,
which our presence caused to be shed—
we saw this clearly, because they
remembered and made us understand
that perhaps in some
deserted place, or on some
mountain, or in some ravine,
our bones were to remain,
our hair was to be scattered, and our
blood was to be spilled. And this
has come to pass for us; it is not fitting
that anyone show a faint heart,
as if he were a fearful and weak
woman. Prepare yourselves like men
to die. Pray to our
Lord God; do not trouble yourselves thinking about..."

fo.3.

[The accompanying Nahuatl text continues the same discourse in the Nahuatl language, recounting the omens encountered along the road — the cries of owls, the howling of coyotes and wild beasts, fires falling, and other signs taken as portents of coming death in war. It conveys the leader's words of comfort to his companions and children, urging them not to grieve or lose heart over these omens, reminding them that sorrow and tears will not change what is destined, and that they must face death bravely, entrusting themselves and their fate to what has been foretold, as true men who do not yield to weakness or despair.]

Book Five

...nothing of this: because soon we shall know, by experience, what is to happen to us at the time we shall see, if some evil is to befall us: then we shall all weep, because this is the glory and fame that we must give and leave to our elders and lords, the noble merchants of great esteem, from whom we descend: for we are not the first, nor are we the last, to whom these things have happened, since many before us and many after us have had the same things befall them: and therefore take courage, like valiant men, my sons. And wherever they came to sleep that day, whether it was under some tree, or under some overhanging rock, or in some cave, then they would gather together all their staffs, or traveling canes that they carried, and bind them all together into one bundle: and then they said that those staffs, all bound together in this way, represented the image of their god Yiacatecutli (who is the god of the merchants and traders). And then, before that bundle of staffs or canes, with great humility and reverence, they would cut their ears, shedding blood, and pierce their tongues, passing...

Here, on the plain, within the ravine, within the forest, everything was scattered: our hair, our locks, slipping away, our blood, our color: for truly it was an afflicted and humbled heart: cast forth death, offer prayer earnestly to our lord: let nothing remain within unremembered; let us know whatever misfortune we strike upon: there, at that very hour, we shall weep greatly: for it is thus that we go forth to honor them, to glorify them, to give light to those who made us, the merchants, the travelers: just as in ancient times they went about, just as they performed their observances — not newly do we show reverence to them, do we gather, do we bind firmly, do we bind all together, do we tie all their staffs into one bundle, setting it where it may be seen. And if anywhere they passed the night, somewhere at the foot of a tree, or at the mouth of a ravine, it is rolled together, it is gathered all into one, it is piled upon the ground, it is assembled, the bundle is tied, it is bound tightly, it is all tied together, all their staffs are gathered as one, and upon it they go forth...

...passing through it willow wands: these, having been bloodied, they offered to the assembly of those staffs, which were all bound together: and all of them resolved to receive with patience, in honor of their god, whatever thing might happen to them from then onward; they would not trouble themselves to think further on it, in case some adverse thing should happen to them because of the omen they had heard from that bird which is called "oactli." And once the term of that omen had passed, if nothing happened to them, they consoled themselves and took heart and courage, because their fright had not come to pass. But some among the company, who were fearful and of little courage, nevertheless went on being afraid that something might happen to them; and so they neither rejoiced nor spoke, nor could they receive consolation; they went about as if fainting and pensive, thinking that something was going to happen to them, and even some distance further on they went on thinking that what had not happened to them yet might, perhaps, near the fulfillment of that omen's meaning, still happen to them by chance.

[Nahuatl parallel text — a corresponding account of the same omen tradition, describing the god Yiacatecutli, the rites of penance and sacrifice performed, the uncertainty and fear felt by the people regarding whether misfortune would come to pass, the dread and loss of peace of mind among the fearful, their ceasing to rejoice, speak, or converse, and their continuing anxious watchfulness as to whether the sign's meaning would yet be fulfilled upon them.]

Book Five

...further on: no one was certain
about what might happen;
because, as was said above,
this omen is indifferent,
being both good and bad.

[decorative floral flourish]

¶ Chapter Three, concerning the omen
they took when they heard at night
some blows, as of someone
cutting wood.

[decorative floral flourish]

¶ When someone at night heard
blows, as of someone chopping wood
at night, they took it as a bad omen; they
called this thing Yoaltepuztli, which
means: nocturnal axe; for the
most part, this sound was heard at
the first sleep of the night, when
everyone was sleeping deeply,
and no sound of people could be heard:
those who went at night to
offer reeds and pine branches heard this sound;
these were ministers of the temple,
who were called tlamacazque. These
had the custom of performing this
exercise, or penance, at night: that is,
in the deepest part of the night, they went to
make these offerings according to custom—

—thus it became an omen: and so
they feared it. This has been told, although no one
knows for certain whether it is true;
perhaps it is only
their own account about it: some say it is good,
and others say it is not good.

¶ This is the third chapter, in which is told
of the omen that used to exist, that used to be
feared: when at night one
heard it, as though someone were splitting wood,
as though someone were chopping with an axe, they
would say, "It is Yoaltepuztli."

Also, there was this omen; people
feared it, it terrified them: it was
called Yoaltepuztli. When it was heard,
everything lay in the deepest sleep,
no one spoke any longer. Those who went to perform penance,
those who went to set out pine branches, the priests
[tlamacazque]—wherever they performed their penance,
upon the mountain, or wherever it might be,
they went, and it was heard
as if someone were splitting, chopping wood: very
far away it could be heard, it was very frightening,
it made the heart die, it made one faint. This,
Yoaltepuztli, thus it is said, so it is told...

Of the omens.

...of the neighboring mountains. And when they heard blows, like someone splitting wood with an axe, which at night could be heard far off, they were frightened by those blows, and took it as a bad omen: they said that these blows were an illusion of Tezcatlipoca, with which he frightened people at night, and made sport of those who walked about at night. And when some brave and courageous man, seasoned in war, heard this, he would not flee, but rather would follow the sound of the blows until he saw what it was; and when he saw some shape of a person, he would run at full speed after it, to catch it and see what it was. It is said that whoever managed to catch hold of this phantom could with difficulty keep hold of it, and so they would run a long time, wandering back and forth from one side to the other. When the phantom pretended to grow tired, the man would wait for it to catch up with him; then he would see what it was that was following him: it was a man without a head, with his neck cut off like a stump, and his chest was open, having on each side something like a little door, which would open and close and strike together in the middle; and in closing, they said, it made those blows that were heard from afar. And whoever this phantom had appeared to — whether he were some brave soldier, or some priest of the temple, courageous in seizing it, and recognizing it by the opening in its chest — would see...

fo. 5.

This one, upon whom it appeared, was Tezcatlipoca: with this he made sport of people, he mocked people, it is said. Whoever saw him, if he was bold, if his heart was steady, if he was not afraid, if his courage held firm, would seize him at once: he would not let him go, so that he might truly see him, might speak with him; he would cling to him, he would hold fast to him, thus he would pursue him: he would follow close behind him, he would chase after him, so that he might truly seize him, might see what manner of thing it was. Thus it is said: whoever managed to seize him and see him found it hard to hold onto him: he kept struggling to get free, moving about everywhere, leading him everywhere until, when he was at last exhausted, somewhere along the road he would let him rest. And when the man looked at him, there he stood, as if his neck had been severed, neck-cut, neck-stumped; and his chest was split open, torn open. Thus it is said: they say that this one, when his chest is heard, it claps shut and opens, it snaps together, it makes a popping sound. And this one, the...

Book Five

...the heart, and thus from him, as if it were being dragged, pulling at it: being in this state, he asked the phantom to grant him some favor, or asked it for some riches, or asked it for strength or valor, so as to capture many in war; and to some it gave what they asked, and to others it did not give what they asked, but rather the opposite, which was poverty, and misery, and bad fortune. And thus they said that it was in the hand of Tezcatlipoca to give whatever thing he wished, whether adverse or prosperous. And the phantom, responding to the request, would speak in this manner: "Gentleman, valiant man, my friend So-and-so, let me go, what do you want of me? For I will give you whatever you wish." And the person to whom this phantom had appeared would say to it: "I will not let you go, for I have already caught you." And the phantom would give him a point, or thorn of maguey, saying to him: "Here, take this thorn, let me go." And he who held the phantom seized by the heart, if he was brave and strong, would not be content with a single thorn; and until he had given him three or four thorns, he would not let it go: these thorns were a sign—

—of whomever it had shown itself to: perhaps it was a priest-offering spirit, or merely something that played tricks on people in all his misfortune. When he had firmly seized it, when he had truly seen it, then his heart raced; he seized it swiftly, he dragged it along, gripping it tightly with his fist, pulling at it: thus he demanded of it what it would give him, what it would bestow on him as a gift, what it would grant him as merit — whether wealth, or captives taken in war, or manly valor; or else poverty, or the digging stick, or the tumpline. Thus it is said, that in this way it used to make men deserving, and their reward would come to be. And it would address the man kindly, saying to him: "My friend, man of war, you are troubling me; what do you ask of me, what do you want from me? Let me go, and I will give you whatever you wish." At once he would give it a name, bestowing on it whatever name, whatever title it should bear. And the commoner to whom it had appeared would say to it: "I will not let you go, for I have already caught you." Thus he would say to it: "Here is a maguey thorn, I give it to you; let me go." He does not accept it, he is not satisfied with it, if his heart is strong and brave; only then does he let it go...

Of the omens.

[The owl] would be fortunate in war, and would take as many captives as the number of thorns he received; and that he would be fortunate and honored in this world, with riches and honors, and with the insignia of a brave man. It was also said that the one whom the phantom seized by the heart, and who was suddenly threatened by it, without saying anything to him, would flee carrying away his heart, and would hide it and guard it with great diligence, wrapping it up and tying it tightly with some cloths. Then the next morning he would unwrap it and look to see what it was that he had pulled out. And if he found something good inside the cloth, such as soft feathers, like cotton, or a few maguey thorns—one or two—this was a sign that good fortune and prosperity would come to him. But if by chance he found in the cloth coals, or some rag, or a piece of torn and dirty cloth, by this he knew that misfortune and misery would come to him. And if the one who heard these nocturnal knockings was a man of little courage and a coward, he would neither pursue it nor go after it, but would tremble with fear and shrink back in terror,

[Nahuatl, parallel text — an account of the nocturnal "tlacacistli" omen:] It cracks, or it hoots, [the owl] gives it the thorn; by this he shows and signifies that he will go to be brave, he will not fear anything. However many thorns were given to him, were handed to him as thorns—by this, there, he merits upon the earth joy and consolation: flowers, tobacco, delight, the cape, the lip-plug, the binding of the hair. It is also said thus, in this account, in this old speech: he who does not speak to [the apparition], it immediately tears out and severs his heart from within him; because of this he trembles and runs, [while] his torn-out heart is carried off somewhere, wrapped up tightly, bound up tightly. When it dawns, he looks at it, he is shown what he has received, the good thing, the fine thing he sees: white down feathers fluffed up, or a thorn, or two, by this it is shown that something good, a reward, has come to be his. But if he does not see something good, but rather coals, or rags, this shows him that only poverty and misery will become his lot. And he who is not at all brave, this...

Book Five

he would throw himself down on all fours, because he could not run nor walk: he thought of nothing else, except that some misfortune was going to befall him, on account of the evil omen he had heard: he thus began at once to fear that sickness or death was going to come upon him, or some misfortune of poverty and hardship, all because of that evil omen.

[Illustration]

Chapter Four, on the evil omen that they took from the song of the owl bird.

Also, when these natives of this New Spain heard the owl sing — whether it was perched upon their house, or upon some tree nearby — upon hearing that manner of the owl's song they immediately became terrified, and they prophesied that some evil was going to come upon them, either sickness, or death, or that some misfortune had already come upon them.

[Nahuatl text, parallel in meaning:] The frightened person does not know, does not recognize [what is happening]; nowhere can he find peace, he only hears it — there where the owl-of-ill-omen screeches, where it hoots and trembles its voice: he can no longer speak well, he is as one half-dead, he becomes faint, his flesh crawls with fear, he can no longer walk properly: thus he knows that the owl's screech has only bewitched him, that with it he has been deceived, with it he has been terrified — whether it be sickness, death, or else misery, affliction, or sin that it has thereby announced to him; thus it befell him.

Fourth chapter, in which is told the omen by which people took evil omens, when the owl cries.

Also, people took omens from this, they regarded it as an evil omen, it was feared as an omen, when the owl cries: when someone hears it crying upon the rooftop, or upon the roof of the hut, or up in a tree, crying outside, saying: "tecolo, o, o, tecolo o o" — thus is its cry heard, thus it cries. They say that when it is heard crying, it reveals [what is to come]...

of the omens.

...had reached the end of life, either someone
of his household, or all of them, or that some
slave would have to flee, or that
someone would come to his house and family
to such great danger that all would
perish, and together the house
would have to be destroyed and left
as a dung heap, a place where
the filth of the human body would be thrown,
and that it would remain as the remnant
of the family and of the house: that is to say. In
this place once lived a person of
great esteem, veneration, and renown:
and now they are no more, only
the walls remain, there is no memory of who
once lived here. In this case, whoever
heard this song of the owl, would immediately
go to someone who would explain these omens,
so that he might be told what
he should do.

fo. 7

Death: sickness, a sign of death:
whoever heard it hoot, perhaps
he would soon die: perhaps there would be war, or
there would be plague, death on the battlefield, or perhaps
death [elsewhere]; or perhaps some nobleman's
child would soon die, or perhaps his servant
would be lost, or perhaps his home would soon be destroyed,
the land would be devastated, the water would disappear, perhaps
it would rain down, the walls would crumble,
the roof beams would fall and scatter, there
people would urinate, void their bowels,
filth and refuse would pile up, saltpeter
would form crusts, the earth would smoke:
then it is said that these marvels occur: thus
it was in that place, in the home where
they came to be frightened: in that place where
they came to be renowned inhabitants: always
wonders were prepared there, misfortunes
were accumulated there: because somewhere
rubbish was being gathered: and at the foot of the house no one
could urinate or defecate: and
now in this place, afterward
it lies abandoned.

Book Five,

Chapter Five, on the bad omen that they took from the hooting of the owl.

When someone, above their house, heard the owl hooting, they took it as a bad omen; they immediately suspected that someone in their house was to die or fall ill — especially if it came two or three times to hoot there over their house. They held their suspicion as confirmed, and if by chance in that house where the owl came to hoot there was already someone sick, they would at once foretell death. They said that the owl was the messenger of the god Mictlan Tecutli, who went and came to the underworld. For this they called it "yautequjua," which means: messenger of the god of the underworld, and goddess of the underworld, who went about summoning those whom she was sent for. And if, together with its hooting, they heard it scratching with its claws, then whoever heard it — if it was a man — they would say to him: "Stay still, you rascal, you've been found out; you committed adultery with your father's wife." And if it was a woman who heard it, they would say to her: "Get out, whore, you've worn a hole in your hair, with which I have something to drink..."

This is the fifth chapter, in which is told the evil omen that existed concerning the owl.

Also feared and dreaded was the owl, or the horned owl: when at night it cries atop the roof, shrieking "cuel" (quickly), they believed that someone there would die — either someone of the household would die, or people would fall sick. And if a second or a third time it shrieked, right there, whether above the roof or inside the house, they would be greatly frightened and troubled; thus they believed it was true, that it was not said in vain, that it would surely come to pass for whomever the owl had cried over. Likewise, if someone was already sick, and it shrieked above them, they said that the person would no longer recover, that they should stop caring for them. For this reason they said, it is told, that the owl was the messenger, the envoy by night, of Mictlan Tecutli and of Mictecacioatl, the two lords of Mictlan; thus they named it "the war-messenger," because it was the companion and envoy of Mictlan Tecutli and Mictecacioatl. And when they heard it cry and rattle its wings, then they would curse it, saying to the owl: "Go on, finish your business, flat-faced owl, go find your mother." And the women said to it, thus...

Of the omens. Page 8.

...there in hell; before this, I cannot go. They said that for this reason they insulted him in this manner: in order to escape the bad omen that he predicted, and so as not to be obliged to fulfill his summons.

The sixth chapter treats of the bad omen that they took when they saw that the weasel, or little mustelid, crossed in front of them when they were walking along the road, or the street.

Of this little animal, which is called weasel, or little mustelid, they were frightened, and they took it as a bad omen: when they saw it enter their house, or cross in front of them; when they were walking along the road, or the street, they conceived in their hearts a bad suspicion that some evil was going to come to them, or that if they were to take some journey, it would not turn out well for them: that they would fall into the hands of thieves, that they would be killed, or that some false testimony would be raised against them. And for this reason, ordinarily those who encountered this little animal had their flesh tremble with fear, and they shuddered, and their hair stood on end; some became rigid, or stunned, believing that some evil was about to happen to them. The form of this animal here in this land is that they are like those of Spain:

[Nahuatl text, chapter six, concerning the omen of the weasel (cozamatl):]

Prologue

Although omens and superstitions seem to be of the same lineage,
omens for the most part attribute to created beings something
that is not in them, as when it is said that when a snake, or weasel,
crosses in front of someone traveling: they say it
is a sign that some misfortune will befall him on the road.
This manner of omens has already been discussed in this fifth book. The
superstitions treated in this appendix are, by contrast, cases where
people take in a bad sense impressions (or influences) that are actually
good for created beings, as when it is said that the scent of the Indian
jasmine, which they call umixuchitl, causes an illness
resembling hemorrhoids. And likewise to the flower called cue-
tlaxuchitl, they attribute a false accusation, saying that when a
woman steps over it, it causes her an illness, which is also
called cuetlaxuchitl, and which occurs in the female member.
And because omens and superstitions are very closely related,
I place this treatise on superstitions as an appendix to this fifth
book on omens. And regarding omens, not everything that occurs
in practice has been said here; nor are all the superstitions
that are wrongly practiced included in this appendix, because
these evil things are always multiplying, and many will find,
regarding one as well as the other, things that are not set down here.

Chapter thirty-six, on the bath, or temazcalli (sweat bath).

Another superstition they held: they said that if a twin entered near the bath while it was being heated, even if it were very hot, it would cool down—and even more so if it was one of the twins themselves who bathed there.
And to remedy this, they would have the person rub the inside of the bath four times with his hand; and with this it would not cool down, but rather heat up more.
Another superstition they held concerning twins: they said that if twins entered where rabbit-hair dye was being prepared, the color would spoil at once, and whatever was being dyed would come out stained, especially the red dye. And to remedy this, they would give the person a little of the water used for dyeing to drink.
Another superstition they held concerning twins: they said that if a twin entered where tamales were cooking, they would immediately spoil them. The same was true of the cooking pot—the tamales could not cook properly even if left on the fire a whole day, and would come out half-cooked, partly done and partly raw. To remedy this, they had the twin himself place the fire under the pot, putting wood beneath it. And if, by chance, tamales had already been placed in the pot before the twin arrived so that they might cook, the twin himself had to put one more into the same pot—otherwise they would not cook at all.

Chapter thirty-seven: concerning when children lose their (baby) teeth.

Another superstition they held concerning the shedding of children's teeth: they said that when a child lost a tooth, the mother or father would throw the fallen tooth into a mouse hole, or have someone else throw it there. They said that if they did not throw it into the mouse hole, a new one would not grow in, and the child would remain toothless.

Here begins the thirty-sixth chapter, which speaks of the temazcalli (sweat bath).

In the temazcalli where people bathe: if someone very hot [with fever or illness] goes there, it is said that his illness worsens; it ruins the bath so that it becomes excessively hot, so that it even seems to stand apart from everyone; it afflicts everyone else who bathes there. And so that it may be cured, it is rubbed four times with the hand, and a potsherd is applied so that the illness will not continue; so that it will only be very hot. Also those who are born as they call "cocoa" (twins): it is said that wherever red dye is made, they must not enter; for if they enter, it is said that the dye will spoil, it will not come out well, it will only come out spotted — especially the bright red. And in order to remedy it, the dye is given a little to drink so that the rabbit hair will not be ruined. Likewise with those called "cocoa" (twins), where tamales are being steamed: they must absolutely not enter there; for it is said that if they enter, the tamales in the pot will also spoil, they will not cook well, even if left the whole day; they will only become half-cooked. And so that this does not happen, when the twin arrives he must himself place the fire under the pot. And if tamales have already been placed there before him, he must place one more among them, so that the tamales will not be ruined.

Here begins the thirty-seventh chapter, which speaks of when children's baby teeth fall out.

When a child's tooth falls out, the mothers throw it into a mouse hole, or they have their children throw it themselves into the mouse hole with their own hands; for it is said that if this is not done, the child's new tooth will not be able to grow in, and he will remain toothless.

These superstitions harm the faith; therefore it is fitting to know them and to preach against them. Only a few have been set down here, though there are many more; but let diligent preachers and confessors seek them out, in order to understand them during confessions, and in order to preach against them — for they are like a mange that infects the faith.
